$comment: SHARED CONTRACT — the MAP SEAM: where the client's answer and the server's answer
must be the same answer. Three invariant families, one file:
7b  map identity keys  — a map_id composed on one side must equal the map_id
composed on the other for identical inputs.
7c  declared-untracked — `transfer_log: "none"` yields an upper bound, and an upper
bound must never be rendered as an exact number.
M4① valid_die_ref      — the referenced map, not circle geometry, is the basis;
with no declaration, behaviour is identical to `2a9f6c4`.
M4② AUTHORING          — the declaration can be SET AND UNSET, and unsetting returns
the map to `circle`. A one-way switch is an operational trap:
`valid_die_ref` lives in metadata a user cannot hand-edit, so
whatever the authoring path cannot undo is undoable by nobody.
Plus the 1-HOP LIMIT: a valid-die map is a map, so it can
itself declare one, and both self-reference and a two-level
chain are refusals.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. In the round that shipped as `2a9f6c4`, two HIGH defects reached
review, and neither was sloppiness: each side was correct in isolation and nobody scored
the ROUND TRIP. This file is scored by BOTH:
server -> contracts/map_seam/test_seam_contract.py   (pytest; self-bootstrapping)
client -> contracts/map_seam/client_harness.mjs      (read-only extraction)
and — this is the point — against THE SAME expected value, never against each other.
PROVENANCE DISCIPLINE. A vector that both sides pass because they share the same wrong
assumption is worth nothing. Every case carries `$source`, which says where its expected
value came from:
spec          — a written rule (MAP_EDITOR_SPEC §5.0 / §6.2-bis, PROJECT_STATUS 8.5)
declared-type — the semantics of the DECLARED column type, which is what makes
INV-7b-2 possible at all (number and string must differ)
measurement   — MEASURED by executing a named commit blob, recorded so that a later
'identical to 2a9f6c4' claim has something to be identical to
invariant     — stated by the round's invariant list; for the M4 cases these were
written BEFORE either implementation existed, deliberately.
No expected value here was copied from whichever implementation was read first.
DECLARED DIVERGENCES live in `*_divergence_cases` with a SEPARATE expectation per
implementation. They are not agreement, and both scorers print them as such.
🔴 NAME THE LAST FUNCTION BEFORE THE DATABASE, AND CHECK IT IS IN THE MANIFEST.
A standing rule for contract review, written 2026-07-29 after a QA NO-GO on M4②, and it
is the most expensive lesson in this file. The contract scored the PURE WRITER
`apply_valid_die_ref` — 402 green assertions, 19 mutations caught, a correct function —
and everyone read that as 'the write path is scored'. It was not. A pure writer only
decides WHAT to write once something else decided a write should happen at all, and that
second decision (`validDieRefForPush`) was in no contract. A HIGH defect lived in the
gap and shipped: an untouched Push silently demoted a cross-table declaration, saving
`{"table":"tpl_map","map_id":"TPL_1"}` as `"TPL_1"` while the chip reported a healthy
reference. Two functions, each correct alone, and nobody scored the pair.
So: before calling a write path scored, trace the value all the way to the payload, name
the LAST function that decides it, and check that name is in `client_symbols` /
`server_symbols`. If it is not there, REPORT THE AXIS AS UNSCORED. A seam is not only
server-versus-client — it is any place two implementations must agree, including two
functions on the same side.
A COROLLARY, learned three times in one day: an UNLISTED CALLEE makes its CALLER
unevaluable, and silently. `validDieRefDisplay` and `validDieRefFromControls` were both
found this way — the extracted function threw, the scorer recorded the exception text as
an answer, and the group was green. Both scorers now treat a thrown extraction as fatal
rather than as a value; that is what turns this class of omission into a red instead of a
false pass.
MISSING SYMBOLS. `client_symbols` / `server_symbols` name every function the contract
needs, and each carries a `status`. The three states mean different things and BOTH
scorers implement them identically — see the `symbol_status` block below for the table
and, more importantly, for why `pending` is allowed to be green and `live` never is.
KNOWN DEFECTS. A failure that is real, understood, and deliberately deferred is PINNED
under a named entry in `known_defects` — never left as an anonymous red. See that block
for the semantics; they are strict, and a pin expires by itself.
THE 2a9f6c4 BASELINE IS NOT RE-MEASURED FROM HEAD, and that is a decision, not an
oversight (asked and answered 2026-07-29, M4 phase 2). `mask_baseline_cases` says what
'unchanged' MEANS, so re-measuring it from the tree that is being changed would turn a
regression gate into a snapshot of whatever the current round happens to ship — the
contract would agree with the code by construction, which is the mirror this file's
provenance rules exist to prevent. Evidence that keeping it costs nothing in accuracy:
`git diff 2a9f6c4 HEAD -- server/utils/` is EMPTY (physical_wafer_engine.py is
byte-identical), so a re-measurement would have produced the same numbers with a worse
provenance. The gate is that TODAY'S engine still reproduces a mask measured before M4
existed, and that is what the scorers run.
THE SHARED SYMBOL VOCABULARY. One table, implemented identically by both scorers —
`test_seam_contract.py::_server_symbol` and `client_harness.mjs`'s manifest loop. Two
scorers with two vocabularies is a mapping table waiting to be written, and a mapping
table is a second implementation of the answer.
status     symbol ABSENT                         symbol PRESENT
live       RENAMED or REMOVED. Hard failure      scored
(client exit 2 / server test fails).
Nothing was compared, and the run
says so rather than narrowing quietly.
pending    PENDING. Reported by name with its     scored AUTOMATICALLY, plus a
owner and the invariants it blocks.    STALE PENDING failure asking for
NOT a failure; the suite stays green.  the one-word promotion to `live`.
required   NOT LANDED. Failure (exit 1).          scored
The axis is overdue, not merely
unscheduled.
WHY `pending` MAY BE GREEN, WHEN NOTHING ELSE HERE MAY BE.
Contract-first is the discipline this file exists to enforce: the vectors for an axis
are written BEFORE the implementation, so the implementer is scored against a spec
nobody reverse-engineered from their own code. But a contract-first vector has nothing
to score yet BY CONSTRUCTION, and rendering that as a hard failure is not rigour — it
is a red suite that means 'working as intended' for days at a time. People learn to
ignore those, and a suite nobody reads is the state `client2/tests/
split_registry_harness.mjs` sat in from U6: dead, comparing nothing, unnoticed.
A reviewer of an UNRELATED round should never have to work out that the red is not
theirs. `pending` is how the file says that in the run output instead of in a chat log.
WHY `pending` STILL EXPIRES BY ITSELF — the three properties, same as a known-defect pin:
1. Before the implementation lands it is QUIET. It does not redden the suite.
2. When it lands it is scored AUTOMATICALLY. The scorers look the symbol up rather
than trusting this field, so nobody has to remember to promote it for the vectors
to start biting. Anything that needs a human to remember is a thing that gets
forgotten.
3. Once it HAS landed, a `status` still reading `pending` is itself a failure.
Not pedantry — it is what preserves rename detection. An absent `pending` symbol
is forgiven by design, so a symbol left at `pending` after landing could later be
renamed or deleted and the contract would silently forgive that too, degrading
back to 'quiet' with the axis unscored. `pending` is a promise to promote, and
property 3 is what collects on it.
A `pending` entry MUST carry `$owner` and `$blocks`. An unowned pending axis is an
anonymous hole with better manners, and `$blocks` is what makes the cost of the wait
legible — both are asserted, not merely requested.
WHERE THE PRESSURE WENT — Lead PM ruling, 2026-07-29, recorded here because a rule that
lives only in a chat log is a rule the next reader does not have. Making `pending` quiet
removes something real: contract-first works BECAUSE the vectors are red until the code
lands, and a quiet pending axis can sit indefinitely. The ruling does not restore the
red. It MOVES the gate:
`pending` does not block the SUITE. It blocks ROUND COMPLETION.
No round is declared finished while any of its `pending` entries is non-zero.
The gate moves from the test runner to the board, where a person holds it. The suite
keeps its meaning — red means something is actually broken, and a reviewer of an
unrelated round never has to work out that the red is not theirs — and the deadline
keeps its teeth. Two different failure modes ('people learn to ignore red' and 'quiet
things get forgotten'), and only the second one has an owner who can be held to it.
THIS IS WHY BOTH SCORERS PRINT PENDING AS A NUMBER rather than as an absence. A count
that never appears in the run output cannot gate anything, and the rule above dies the
first time someone reads a green summary and stops there. `pending` is the number the
Lead PM reads before calling a round done, so both scorers report
pass / fail / pending as three separate figures.
NAMED, ATTRIBUTED, SELF-CANCELLING pins for failures that are real, understood, and
deliberately not fixed in this round.
WHY A REGISTRY AND NOT JUST A RED. A permanent anonymous red is worse than no contract
at all: people stop reading it, and a contract nobody reads stops being evidence about
anything. `client2/tests/split_registry_harness.mjs` sat DEAD from U6 — dying in its own
extraction step, comparing nothing — and nobody noticed, because nobody was reading it.
That is the failure mode this block exists to prevent, and the reason a pin must expire
on its own rather than depend on someone remembering it.
SEMANTICS ARE STRICT. Three outcomes per pinned assertion, and only the first is green:
client == `client_actual`  -> PINNED. Reported under its defect id with the recorded
disagreement, not as an anonymous divergence.
client == the contract     -> STALE PIN. The contract goes RED IN THE OTHER DIRECTION.
The defect was fixed and nobody removed the pin, so this
vector has silently stopped asserting the contract value.
client == neither          -> the defect CHANGED SHAPE. Also red, and louder.
A PIN MAY NOT BE SELF-SATISFYING. Both scorers assert that every `client_actual` DIFFERS
from the contract value it stands in for. A pin that agrees with the contract asserts
nothing and would be a way to make any vector permanently green by writing it twice.
PINS ARE CLIENT-SCOPED BY CONSTRUCTION. The key is `$client_known_defect`, and the server
scorer keeps asserting the CONTRACT value on the very same vectors (and asserts that no
pin ever claims the server side). That asymmetry is what makes the recorded value
evidence of a real disagreement rather than a label pasted over a red.

D1.title: physNum substitutes the default for a legitimately declared 0
statement: `return v || dflt` (line 1547 — DOM arm) and `return ov || dflt` (line 1544 — frame-override
arm) are FALSY tests, so a declared 0 is indistinguishable from an absent value and is
replaced by the default. Of the six call sites only `edgeMargin` has a non-zero default
(3.0), so it is the one where a legitimate declaration is destroyed: `phys_edge_margin: 0`
silently becomes 3.0mm and every geometry derived from the effective radius moves with it.
The source comment above the function calls the behaviour a preserved convention
('0 -> 기본값'), which is why it survived review: it reads as intent, not as a bug.
D1.predates_evidence: `git show 2a9f6c4:client2/src/map_editor.js` carries the same eight lines at 1402-1409. This round did not introduce it and is not scored for it.
D1.server_is_correct: map_overlay._frame_phys_params reads a declared 0 as 0. The two sides therefore disagree about the wafer mask itself for any site declaring a zero margin — this is a SEAM defect, not a cosmetic one.
D1.impact: effective_radius = dia/2 - 3.0 instead of dia/2. On the 20mm declaration below that is 7.0mm where the contract says 10.0mm, and cells the server counts as valid dies are drawn — and painted — as outside the wafer.
why_not_fixed_in_this_round: The fix MOVES STORED COORDINATES. `getWaferBoundingBox` (map_editor.js:1672) calls
`isCellInsideWaferFast` directly at :1703, and the persisted x/y are derived from that
bounding box — so widening the effective radius re-indexes every cell of every affected
map. That needs its own round plus a data audit of which maps carry `phys_edge_margin: 0`.
Pinning it here is not tolerance: it is refusing to let a coordinate migration ride along

valid_die_ref_for_push.$blocks: valid_die_push_decision_cases — the LAST decision before the DB.
valid_die_ref_for_push.$why: 🔴 ADDED 2026-07-29 AFTER A QA NO-GO, and the omission is the lesson. This contract scored the PURE WRITER (`applyValidDieRef`) at 402 green assertions and everyone — me included — read that as 'the write path is scored'. It was not. `applyValidDieRef` only decides WHAT to write once someone has decided IT SHOULD WRITE AT ALL, and that second decision lives here. A HIGH defect lived in the gap: `syncValidDieRefControls` forces an out-of-list declaration table to `''`, this function reads that `''` as 'the user chose the home table', and an UNTOUCHED Push silently demoted a cross-table declaration — `{"table":"tpl_map","map_id":"TPL_1"}` saved as `"TPL_1"`, table gone, chip still reporting a healthy reference. Both halves were correct in isolation; nobody scored the pair. That is the same shape as the two HIGH defects that created this file.
valid_die_ref_for_push.$rule: AT CONTRACT REVIEW, NAME THE LAST FUNCTION THAT DECIDES THE VALUE ACTUALLY SENT TO THE DB AND CHECK IT IS IN THIS MANIFEST. If it is not, report the axis as UNSCORED — do not let a green pure-writer stand in for a scored write path.
valid_die_ref_for_push.$shape: `validDieRefForPush() -> {keep: true} | {keep: false, ref}`. Reads module state `validDie.raw` and the DOM controls; not pure, which is why the scorer drives it through `syncValidDieRefControls` instead of writing control values itself.

valid_die_ref_payload.$blocks: valid_die_push_decision_cases — while this was absent the scorer reproduced the Push glue instead of running it.
valid_die_ref_payload.$landed: 2026-07-29 (map-pm), map_editor.js; called from the Push site. Promoted pending -> live and the scorer's duplicated glue DELETED in the same pass — an extraction that lands while the scorer keeps its copy buys nothing, because the copy is what would go stale. THE FULL CYCLE THIS STATUS EXISTS FOR RAN ONCE, END TO END, INSIDE ONE ROUND: declared `pending` (quiet, suite green) -> Lead PM held ROUND COMPLETION rather than the runner -> map-pm extracted -> scored AUTOMATICALLY on landing, because the scorers look the symbol up instead of trusting this field -> not promoted, so STALE PENDING billed for it. All three designed properties fired.
valid_die_ref_payload.$why: AN EXTRACTION REQUEST, not a missing feature. The two lines at the Push site that turn `validDieRefForPush()`'s decision into the `grid_metadata` actually sent — `decision.keep ? {...gridMeta, valid_die_ref: validDie.raw} : applyValidDieRef(gridMeta, decision.ref)` — are LOGIC, and they sit inside a long DOM-bound Push function no scorer can reach. So the contract re-types them, and a scorer that re-types logic can drift from it silently. Extracting them into one pure function makes the composition scoreable by RUNNING it, which is the same move that made INV-7c-2 scoreable (`transfer_log_is_declared_none`) and the same one that made the write path scoreable at all (`applyValidDieRef`). Quiet by design until it lands; by the Lead PM's 2026-07-29 ruling it blocks ROUND COMPLETION rather than the suite.
valid_die_ref_payload.$shape: PURE `validDieRefPayload(gridMeta, decision, raw) -> gridMeta` (argument order the implementer's call) — the single place the Push decision becomes the stored payload.

valid_die_ref_from_controls.$blocks: valid_die_push_decision_cases — `validDieRefForPush` calls it, so without it the extracted decision THROWS.
valid_die_ref_from_controls.$why: A CALLEE, and the third one this contract has had to add after the fact (`validDieRefDisplay`, then this). Listing it is not bookkeeping: an unlisted callee makes its CALLER unevaluable, and the failure is silent unless something makes a thrown extraction fatal — see `threw()` in the harness. It also carries the fix's real mechanism: the declared table is read from the control ONLY when `validDieRefTableTouched` says the user actually opened the select, which is what stops a forced-blank select from being read as a deliberate choice.
valid_die_ref_from_controls.$shape: `validDieRefFromControls() -> {shown, table, key}`. Reads `validDie.raw`, the controls, and the module flag `validDieRefTableTouched`.

sync_valid_die_ref_controls.$blocks: valid_die_push_decision_cases — it is the only legitimate way to put the controls into a state the app can actually produce.
sync_valid_die_ref_controls.$why: The OTHER half of the same pair, and it is in the manifest for a reason beyond being a callee. The round harness set `el.validDieRefTable.value = table` directly, skipping this function, and so asserted a control state THE APP CANNOT PRODUCE — green, and blind to the entire contract between the two functions. A scorer that writes the control values is testing its own fixture. This contract sets `validDie.raw` and the option LIST, then calls this function, exactly as the app does.
