canonical_value_cases.name: num_unreadable
canonical_value_cases.$why: MAP_EDITOR_SPEC §5.0: an unreadable value keeps its trimmed original so the lookup misses HONESTLY. `Number('0x10')` is 16 in JS while Python's `float('0x10')` raises — a readability test built on Number() would invent the key '16' on one side only. This vector is what forces the decimal-only test.

canonical_value_cases.name: str_padded
canonical_value_cases.$why: INV-7b-2, the load-bearing half: under `string` the padding IS the identity. '01' must NOT become '1' — if it did, the declared type would be decoration.

canonical_value_cases.name: str_float_text
canonical_value_cases.$why: Text '1.0' under a string declaration is data, not a repr artifact — contrast `num_float_text`: same text, different answer. This pair is what proves the two types behave differently.

canonical_value_cases.name: str_trim_collides
canonical_value_cases.$why: Trim ONLY. Whitespace is transport noise; a leading zero is not.

canonical_value_cases.name: undeclared_padded
canonical_value_cases.$why: No declaration = string semantics. Guessing `number` would silently merge keys in every table that has not declared its types.

$comment: Scored on the SERVER only, and the reason is a transport fact rather than an exemption:
the client's key values originate as DOM input strings and JSON text, so these inputs
cannot reach `canonicalKeyValue`. Scoring them would pin cross-language coercion trivia
(`String(true)` is 'true', `str(True)` is 'True') that no real input can produce.

canonical_value_server_only_cases.name: bool_is_not_a_number
canonical_value_server_only_cases.$why: bool is not an integer: int-casting True to '1' would collide with slot 1.

canonical_value_server_only_cases.name: none_stays_none
canonical_value_server_only_cases.$why: None is not a key. Composition sites decide their own placeholder — and, per compose_divergence_cases, they decide DIFFERENTLY.

$comment: INV-7b-3 — THE SEAM. Both sides are scored against `expect_map_id`; neither is scored
against the other. INV-7b-1 is the `slot_number_*` block: four spellings, one key.
INV-7b-2 is the `slot_string_*` block: the SAME four spellings, three keys. Read the two
blocks side by side — that contrast IS the contract.

compose_cases.name: slot_number_float_text
compose_cases.$why: INV-7b-1 complete: these four rows must all read LOT_1. The operational bug was exactly this — the client composed LOT_01, storage held LOT_1, and the map opened while its metadata looked absent.

compose_cases.name: slot_string_padded
compose_cases.$why: INV-7b-2. Same input as `slot_number_padded`, different declared type, DIFFERENT key. If these two ever agree, the declaration stopped being read.

compose_cases.name: slot_string_spaced
compose_cases.$why: Trim still applies under `string` — whitespace is transport noise on both types.

compose_cases.name: undeclared_table
compose_cases.$why: A table with no declaration must not be guessed into `number`. Silent merging across every undeclared table is worse than a miss.

compose_cases.name: three_component_key
compose_cases.$why: map_key_columns is not always 2. Every component canonicalizes by its OWN declared type.

compose_cases.name: lot_number_declared
compose_cases.$why: The FIRST component canonicalizes too. A fix applied only to `slot` passes every other case in this group.

$comment: DECLARED DIVERGENCE — not agreement. A missing or empty key component is handled three
different ways ON PURPOSE, each documented at its own call site:
map_overlay.compose_map_id        -> '' placeholder, so 'LOT_'   (map_overlay.py:199)
map_meta_registrar.compose_map_id -> None: refuse to register a partial identity
(map_meta_registrar.py:150, explicit comment)
client getMapIdFromMeta           -> drops the blank column, so 'LOT'
Each is scored against ITS OWN documented answer, so any one changing is caught. What is
NOT asserted is that they agree — because they do not. The consequence is stated for the
Lead PM in the report: a client-composed 'LOT' can never match anything the registrar
wrote, because the registrar declined to write it. That is a safe miss today; it stops
being safe the moment any writer starts composing partial identities.
INV-7b-4, forward direction: a stored map_id decomposes to per-column bind values. Both
sides split on '_' with the LAST declared column absorbing the remainder, then canonicalize
each part by its declared type — so a padded '01' typed into a search box still finds a
number-declared column storing 1.
The inverse property is DERIVED in both scorers from `compose_cases` rather than restated
here, so it cannot drift away from the composition it claims to invert.

decompose_cases.name: undecomposable_falls_to_first_column
decompose_cases.$why: Fewer parts than columns: both sides match the WHOLE key against the first column rather than inventing an empty second component (MAP_EDITOR_SPEC §6.4 LOAD parity). A vector here because 'what happens when it does not fit' is where two implementations usually part ways.

$comment: The last hole 7b left, and a direct seam pair: an ALREADY-ASSEMBLED key string arriving
from outside (a declaration, a parsed token, a URL) may not be canonical. `compose_map_id`
cannot help — it canonicalizes components, not a finished string. Cell filters survive
because they cast by column type; `load_map_meta` is exact string equality and misses
silently. Server `canonical_map_key` and client `canonicalMapKey` must agree character
for character, because their output IS the lookup key.
Idempotence is DERIVED in both scorers: canon(canon(k)) == canon(k) for every case.

canonical_map_key_cases.name: string_slot_untouched
canonical_map_key_cases.$why: INV-7b-2 at the string level: the same key text canonicalizes differently under the two declarations, or the declaration is not being read.

canonical_map_key_cases.name: unreadable_part_preserved
canonical_map_key_cases.$why: An unreadable component keeps its trimmed original so the lookup misses honestly. Inventing 'LOT_16' would find the WRONG map, which is worse than finding none.

$comment: INV-7b-4's BOUNDARY, stated rather than hidden. Both sides let the LAST column absorb the
remainder, so composition is invertible only when no component EXCEPT the last contains
the separator. A lot named 'LOT_A' with slot '1' composes to 'LOT_A_1' and decomposes to
lot='LOT', slot='A_1' — a different map.
Both sides are scored against the same lossy answer, so they at least MISS TOGETHER rather
than landing on two different maps. Whether the absorb-last rule should change is a
contract question for the Lead PM, not something a harness may decide. Note that the
source comment on BOTH sides says the rule defends lot names containing '_', which is the
opposite of what it does — absorbing into the LAST column defends the LAST component.

decompose_lossy_cases.name: separator_in_lot
decompose_lossy_cases.$why: Measured from both implementations; recorded so a future change is visible, NOT endorsed.

decompose_lossy_cases.name: separator_in_slot
decompose_lossy_cases.$why: The case the absorb-last rule actually protects — separator in the LAST component.

$comment: INV-7c-3 — N in '≤N' is total − fail, and it stays a genuine UPPER BOUND. Scored against
`transfer_plan.build_chips_block`, which is pure, so no fixture is needed.
The rule under test: dropping a SUBTRACTION term can only raise the result, so the
computed value bounds the true remaining from above — but only while the TOTAL is still
trustworthy. Once the denominator itself is degraded the number bounds nothing and must
not be called a bound.

chips_bound_cases.name: untracked_only
chips_bound_cases.$why: The 7c happy path. 92 = 100 − 8 = total − fail. `remaining` stays null because it is not known; the bound carries the information under its own name.

chips_bound_cases.name: untracked_plus_total_degraded
chips_bound_cases.$why: INV-7c-3's teeth. A second degradation hits the TOTAL, so the same arithmetic no longer bounds anything. Serving 92 here would be a confident-looking number with no claim behind it.

chips_bound_cases.name: fully_reliable
chips_bound_cases.$why: The control. An exact remaining must NOT also ship a bound — two numbers for one quantity is how a reader picks the wrong one.

chips_bound_cases.name: negative_remaining_is_not_a_bound
chips_bound_cases.$why: A negative value is not an upper bound on a quantity that cannot go below zero — it is evidence of population mismatch. '≤ −10' would be nonsense wearing a contract's clothes.

chips_bound_cases.name: zero_bound_is_a_real_bound
chips_bound_cases.$why: 0 is a bound, not an absence. Dropping it for being falsy would turn 'at most none left' into 미상.

$comment: INV-7c-2 at the CONFIG boundary — the site's declaration itself. Was PENDING; the named
predicate `transfer_plan.transfer_log_is_declared_none` LANDED 2026-07-29 (transfer_plan.py:276)
and these vectors are now scored. While it was pending they were reported NOT LANDED and the
server run exited non-zero — never skipped, because a contract the code does not meet yet is
a red contract, and that is exactly how it got built.

transfer_log_declaration_cases.name: title_none
transfer_log_declaration_cases.$why: The most likely typo and the one with the worst payoff: 'None' promoted would turn every mis-cased config into a claim of knowledge.

transfer_log_declaration_cases.name: json_null
transfer_log_declaration_cases.$why: null is indistinguishable from an accidentally deleted key — it cannot carry a declaration.

transfer_log_declaration_cases.name: table_named_none
transfer_log_declaration_cases.$why: A real binding object, not a declaration. Any truthiness or membership test confuses the two.

$comment: INV-7c-1 — CLIENT ONLY (the server renders nothing). Scored through the two functions
that decide it: `untrackedBoundOf(entry)` -> number|null and `boundText(bound)` -> string.
The load-bearing assertion is the NEGATIVE one, and both are checked: where a bound exists
the text must contain '≤' AND must not equal the bare number. '≤12' and '12' are one
character apart and say opposite things about whether the operator may trust the figure.

remaining_display_cases.name: declared_bound_zero
remaining_display_cases.$why: Pairs with chips_bound_cases.zero_bound_is_a_real_bound: a 0 bound must survive rendering too. A `if (!bound)` guard drops it and shows 미상.

remaining_display_cases.name: degraded_without_declaration
remaining_display_cases.$why: Degradation WITHOUT a declaration stays 미상. 7c must not turn every degradation into a cheerful bound.

remaining_display_cases.name: declared_but_server_withheld_the_bound
remaining_display_cases.$why: Declared untracked AND something else degraded, so the server deliberately withheld the bound. The client must not reconstruct one from total − fail; a second implementation of that arithmetic is the divergence this whole file exists to stop.

remaining_display_cases.name: bound_as_string_is_not_a_number
remaining_display_cases.$why: A stringified bound means something reserialised the response. Coercing it would render '≤12' from a payload nobody validated.

remaining_display_cases.name: bin_absent
remaining_display_cases.$why: 'this BIN is not on this map' is not 'none left' (DOE_BAND_MODEL §4-bis): the operator must act differently.

$comment: INV-7c-2 ON THE WIRE — CLIENT ONLY. The server declares the state by putting
`transfer_untracked: true` on the entry, so the client never parses the config string.
What it must do is read the flag STRICTLY: only the JSON boolean `true` promotes the
reading to a bound. Same discipline `map_push_ok` already carries (`is True` on the
server, `=== true` on the client) and for the same reason — a truthy test lets the string
"false", a stray 1, or a config typo promote a broken binding into a confident number.
Every non-true spelling below carries a real bound in the entry precisely so a truthy
implementation would render '≤12' and get caught.

untracked_flag_cases.name: string_false
untracked_flag_cases.$why: The nastiest one: non-empty, so every truthy test promotes it, and it says the opposite of what it would then mean.

$comment: M4 INV-M4-1 — 'no ref -> behaviour identical to 2a9f6c4' needs something to be identical
TO. Every `mask` below was MEASURED by executing `is_cell_inside_wafer` out of the
`2a9f6c4` git blob (not the working tree) over the frame grid, after the declared metadata
passed through `map_overlay._frame_phys_params`.
'#' = inside, '.' = outside, one string per frame row, row 0 first.
The client is scored against the SAME strings through its own real parse chain
(`physNum` -> `getTransformedPhysicalConfig` -> `getScreenShift` -> `isCellInsideWaferFast`),
not through a hand-built physConfig: the parse is part of the seam, and it is where the
two sides were measured to disagree.
`declared` is the metadata as a site declares it. `canvas` is the client's pixel viewport —
the client works in screen space and the server in millimetres, so the mask must come out
the same at every canvas size or the geometry is viewport-dependent.

mask_baseline_cases.name: r9_offset_rot0_back
mask_baseline_cases.$why: `side: back` flips the sign of the x offset BEFORE rotation on both sides. Front and back differ here, so a side-blind implementation cannot pass both.

mask_baseline_cases.name: r9_offset_rot90_front
mask_baseline_cases.$why: Rotation swaps the chip pitches into frame axes AND permutes the offsets. The server holds that as a 4-row table in `_frame_phys_params`; the client holds it in `getTransformedPhysicalConfig` + `getScreenShift`. Two tables, one answer required.

mask_baseline_cases.name: margin_zero_declared
mask_baseline_cases.$why: A site declaring NO edge exclusion. effective_radius = 20/2 − 0 = 10 — the engine's stated formula applied to the stated declaration, so the expected value comes from the DECLARATION, not from either implementation. This vector was known to fail on the client when it was written, which is exactly why it is here; that failure is now pinned as D1.

$client_known_defect.$why_here: The DIRECT expression of D1: the only difference between this case and `r7_sym_rot0` is `edge_margin: 0` instead of 3, and that one field is what the client throws away. Server passes; client is 3mm short of the declaration.
$client_known_defect.$evidence: Contract radius 10.0 vs client 7.0 — exactly the 3.0mm default D1 substitutes. The masks are COUNTED, not eyeballed: 37 cells inside per the declaration, 13 on the client. 24 dies the server counts as real are drawn, and painted, as outside the wafer.

mask_baseline_cases.name: tangent_exact
mask_baseline_cases.$why: Chosen so a cell corner lands EXACTLY on the radius: cell (3,2) has corner (3,4) at distance exactly 5 = R (a 3-4-5 triangle, every value exactly representable in binary). The predicate is '<= R', so it is inside — but only if both sides round the same way, and they compute in different units (mm vs pixels). Knife-edge cells are where the '373 of 1293' incidents lived.

$client_known_defect.$why_here: Same cause, worse blast radius, and the reason this pin is worth reading. This case also declares `edge_margin: 0`, so D1 shrinks R from 5.0 to 2.0 — and with `chip_y: 8` NOTHING fits inside 2.0mm. The client reports an ENTIRELY EMPTY wafer for a map the contract says has three valid dies.
$client_known_defect.$evidence: 3 cells inside per the declaration, 0 on the client. Note what a pin does NOT by itself claim: that fixing the defect makes the case pass. This is the knife-edge vector (corner exactly on R, mm vs pixels), so D1 MASKS its rounding axis — the client never gets close enough to the boundary for that axis to be observed at all.
$client_known_defect.$masked_axis: knife-edge '<= R' rounding parity between mm and pixel space
$client_known_defect.$masked_axis_measured: 2026-07-29, in an isolated copy with both physNum arms fixed: the client then produces the CONTRACT mask ['.....','.....','.###.','.....','.....'] and radius 5.0 at 700px. So the knife-edge axis does agree across the seam, and D1 is the ONLY cause of this vector's failure. Recorded because a pin whose blast radius was guessed at is a pin nobody can act on — but it is a measurement of a hypothetical tree, not a promise: re-run the case when D1 is really fixed.

$comment: ── ANISOTROPY, and why these three vectors exist ──────────────────────────────────
Everything above this line was BLIND to the chip-pitch swap, and it was blind by
construction rather than by oversight. map-pm measured it: swap the declared `chip_x`
and `chip_y` in every mask vector above and count the cells that move.
r7_sym_rot0 + all nine r9_offset_* + margin_zero_declared  ->  0 cells move
tangent_exact                                              ->  0 cells move
Nine of them declare a SQUARE chip (2.5 x 2.5), so a pitch swap is undetectable no
matter what the implementation does. `tangent_exact` is genuinely anisotropic (2 x 8) —
but D1 collapses its radius to 2mm, so its mask is empty either way and it is blind for
a second, unrelated reason.
The consequence, stated plainly: an implementation that FAILS TO SWAP THE PITCH on a
quarter turn moved zero cells across the whole fixture set. Four cases carried rotation
90/270 and all four were nominal coverage — a vector both sides pass because neither is
being asked the question. Rotation permutes chip_x/chip_y into the frame axes, the
server holds that as a 4-row table in `_frame_phys_params` and the client as
`getTransformedPhysicalConfig` + `getScreenShift`, and NOTHING was scoring the swap.
`tangent_exact_rot90` closes it on the server. It does NOT close it on the client,
because it inherits D1 and is pinned to an empty mask — a pitch-blind client would
still pass it. That is why the `aniso_quarter_turn_*` pair follows: the SAME geometry
(R = 5.0, chip 2 x 8) reached through a declaration D1 cannot touch (dia 16, margin 3,
so the falsy-0 substitution is a no-op). Those two are live on both sides TODAY, and
their masks are transposes of each other — read them as a pair, the contrast IS the
assertion. Both scorers additionally RUN the swap and require the mask to move, so the
axis cannot go quietly nominal again.

mask_baseline_cases.name: tangent_exact_rot90
mask_baseline_cases.$why: The quarter turn of `tangent_exact`, and the transpose of its mask: the 2mm pitch runs along the frame's x axis at rot0 and along its y axis at rot90. An implementation that applies the declared pitches without permuting them by rotation reproduces the rot0 mask here and fails. Measured 2026-07-29 through `_frame_phys_params` + `PhysicalWaferEngine`, cross-checked against the `2a9f6c4` engine blob (identical).

$client_known_defect.$why_here: Inherits `tangent_exact`'s zero margin, so D1 shrinks R from 5.0 to 2.0 here too and the client's mask is empty. Pinned rather than dropped: it is the SERVER's quarter-turn anisotropy assertion, and it becomes the client's the day D1 clears.
$client_known_defect.$evidence: 3 cells inside per the declaration, 0 on the client — the same shape as `tangent_exact`, from the same cause. NOTE what this pin costs while it stands: a pitch-blind CLIENT still passes this vector, because empty equals empty. `aniso_quarter_turn_rot90` below is the vector that actually holds the client to the swap today.

mask_baseline_cases.name: aniso_quarter_turn_rot0
mask_baseline_cases.$why: Geometrically identical to `tangent_exact` (16/2 − 3 = 5.0 = 10/2 − 0) but declared so that D1 CANNOT reach it: with a non-zero margin the falsy-0 substitution is a no-op. That is the entire point of the pair — the anisotropy axis had to survive independently of a defect that is not being fixed this round, or it would have been pinned into invisibility on the client and 'covered' on paper. Two canvas sizes because the client works in pixels and the server in millimetres.

mask_baseline_cases.name: aniso_quarter_turn_rot90
mask_baseline_cases.$why: The load-bearing half, and the first vector in this file that a pitch-blind client fails. Its mask is the transpose of `aniso_quarter_turn_rot0`: swap the two declared pitches and 4 of the 25 cells move. Both scorers assert that movement directly rather than trusting these two literals to disagree.

$comment: M4 INV-M4-3, and the axis that is PURE on both sides so the seam is directly scoreable.
The rule, one sentence: only `null`/absent means 'no declaration'; everything else IS a
declaration and an unreadable one must ERROR, never quietly become 'no declaration'.
Folding an unreadable declaration into absence is exactly the silent fallback to circle
geometry INV-M4-3 forbids — one typo and a wrong answer becomes indistinguishable from a
right one.
Three outcomes, and the vectors name which: `none` (no declaration) | `ref` (resolved) |
`error` (declared but unreadable). Field names differ across the seam by language
convention (`map_id` server / `mapKey` client); the scorers normalise, and the TABLE and
KEY values are compared, which is what a lookup actually uses.
TABLE DIVERGENCE, DECLARED 2026-08-04 (map request 1-a, user ruling): the CLIENT load
path is PINNED — "불러오기는 무조건 valid_die_ref 를 이용하게". So on every `ref`
vector the two sides now answer the table differently and BOTH answers are recorded:
`expect_table`        — the server's answer (`server/map_overlay.parse_valid_die_ref`),
which is still the storage format's original meaning: a bare
string is 'a map in MY table'.
`expect_client_table` — the client's answer, which is the pinned constant and nothing
else (`client_consts` VALID_DIE_TABLE).
The KIND and the KEY do NOT diverge, and that is the point: the pin changed WHERE the
client looks, not what counts as a declaration. Every `ref` vector must carry
`expect_client_table` — the client scorer FAILS on a ref vector that omits it, so a
vector added later cannot silently stop covering the pin.
This divergence is OPEN and belongs to the server lane: until `map_overlay` is pinned
too, a server-resolved basis and a client-resolved basis for the same legacy row name
different maps. Recorded here rather than decided here.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: explicit_null
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: A null declaration is indistinguishable from a deleted key, so it is absence — the ONE shape allowed to mean 'behave exactly as 2a9f6c4'.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: string_inherits_home_table
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: The commonest use: another map of the same table. Inheriting the declaring map's table is the same convention overlay `sources` already uses.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: empty_string_is_an_error
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: Empty is a BROKEN declaration, not an absent one. Treating it as absence is the silent fallback.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: object_full
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: The sharpest case for the pin: the declaration EXPLICITLY names another table and the client still reads valid_die_ref. Nothing is rewritten on disk — the row keeps saying tpl_table (valid_die_push_decision_cases proves that) — but the lookup goes to the fixed table and refuses BY NAME when the key is not there.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: object_alias_names
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: `target_table`/`map_key` are wafer_map_metadata's real column names and `table`/`map_id` the short aliases — one pair, two spellings. Both sides accept both, and NOTHING ELSE: guessing further names would resolve a typo to a real map.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: object_missing_map_id
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: A table with no key names no map. Inheriting the declaring map's own key here would make a map its own valid-die template — circular and silently self-satisfying.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: array_is_an_error
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: An array is a plausible-looking hand edit. In JS `typeof [] === 'object'`, so a bare typeof check accepts it and reads undefined fields — this vector is what forces the explicit Array check.

valid_die_ref_parse_cases.name: boolean_is_an_error
valid_die_ref_parse_cases.$why: `true` reads like 'yes, use a valid-die ref' and names no map. It must refuse, not resolve to something.

$comment: DECLARED DIVERGENCE, found by this contract on the round trip and reported to the Lead PM
rather than decided here: a declaration that names NO table when the caller supplied no
home table either. Both sides are internally consistent and they disagree on the answer.
This is a contract question, not a bug report — which is why the resolution is the Lead
PM's call and this file only records both answers.
CLOSED 2026-08-04 on the KIND axis by the load pin (map request 1-a). The client used to
error here because it had no table to look in; pinned, it always has one, so the branch
that produced the error no longer exists and both sides now say `ref`. The group is kept
— not deleted — because the TABLE still diverges (see valid_die_ref_parse_cases) and
because a group deleted when it goes green stops noticing when it comes back.

valid_die_ref_home_divergence_cases.name: object_no_table_no_home
valid_die_ref_home_divergence_cases.$why: WAS `error` on the client until 2026-08-04. The pin removed the 'target table unknown' branch outright — under a fixed table the target cannot become unknown — so this half of the divergence closed as a side effect rather than by a decision about it.

valid_die_ref_home_divergence_cases.name: string_no_home
valid_die_ref_home_divergence_cases.$why: The control for the case above: on the STRING form both sides accept a missing table. Keeping it here shows the divergence is specific to the object form, not to 'no home table' generally.

$comment: M4 INV-M4-1 / INV-M4-2 / INV-M4-3 at the branch point. Expected values come from the
round's stated invariants, written before either implementation existed.
Contract: `resolve_valid_die_basis(meta, resolver, table)` -> {basis, source, reason},
source in circle|ref|refused, and `reason` non-empty whenever source is `refused`.
`resolver` is a stub here: the point is WHICH BASIS WINS, not how cells are fetched.
SCORED ON BOTH SIDES as of 2026-07-29. It was SERVER_ONLY before, on the reasoning that
'the basis branch is server-side this round' — which stopped being true when the client
grew `validDieBasis` + `isValidDieAt`. The two most load-bearing M4 invariants were then
unscored on the client, on a contract whose entire purpose is that neither side is scored
alone. The client half is reached through the branch point, not the resolver: the network
walk that fills the state is not the contract, WHICH BASIS WINS is.
ONE SEAM, ONE VOCABULARY: `circle` | `ref` | `refused`. The server already returns exactly
these from `resolve_valid_die_basis`, so they are canonical and the client's `map` /
`unresolved` spelling is the one that moves. This is a Lead PM ruling, recorded here
rather than in a chat log: two vocabularies on one seam is how a mapping table gets
written, and a mapping table is a second implementation of the answer.
The token is therefore CONTRACT SURFACE, not an internal detail — the client scorer
injects state using the canonical spelling, so a half-done rename fails loudly.
WHAT THE CLIENT RENDERS ON `refused` is a DECLARED DIVERGENCE, and it lives in its own
group — `valid_die_refused_render_divergence_cases` below. The vectors here score WHICH
BASIS WINS on both sides; they deliberately do not decide what a canvas does with it.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: no_declaration_is_circle
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: INV-M4-1, additive coexistence. A map with no `valid_die_ref` behaves exactly as at 2a9f6c4, and the mask it must reproduce is the MEASURED baseline named here rather than a restatement of it.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: ref_is_the_sole_basis
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: INV-M4-2. `(40,40)` is deliberately OUTSIDE any circle this metadata could describe: an implementation that intersects ref with circle geometry drops it and fails here. Intersecting looks conservative while silently discarding dies the template declares valid — which is the defect class M4 exists to remove.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: unresolvable_ref_refuses
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: INV-M4-3. Falling back to circle geometry would produce a plausible map from a broken declaration and the operator would never learn the reference was wrong.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: resolver_raises_refuses
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: A resolver that throws is an unresolved reference, not an absent one. Letting the exception escape into a generic handler that returns the circle is the same silent fallback wearing a stack trace.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: empty_cell_set_refuses
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: Zero cells is 'not loaded yet', not 'no die is valid'. Accepting it as an answer invalidates the user's entire map — the loudest possible wrong answer, arrived at silently.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: unreadable_declaration_refuses
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: Ties valid_die_ref_parse_cases to the branch: a declaration that fails to parse must reach `refused`, not `circle`.

valid_die_basis_cases.name: declared_without_resolver_refuses
valid_die_basis_cases.$why: A caller that cannot resolve references must not be silently served circle geometry for a map that declared otherwise.

$comment: DECLARED DIVERGENCE — the two sides answer `refused` differently, ON PURPOSE, and the
asymmetry is structural rather than a disagreement anyone can fix.
server  `resolve_valid_die_basis` -> {source: 'refused', basis: None}. It CAN return
'no mask', because nothing is being drawn.
client  cannot. A canvas with no mask is not a renderable state, so it renders the
pre-M4 CIRCLE (map_editor.js:1938 — the verdict the caller already computed
passes straight through) and marks the refusal in three places: the status-bar
chip, a toast, and the console.
WHY THIS IS PINNED AND NOT LEFT AS PROSE. Scoring only the `source` string — which is
all `valid_die_basis_cases` did — leaves nothing asserting that the refusal is SURFACED.
A future change could turn that visible refusal into a silent circle fallback and every
vector in this file would stay green: the source string would still read 'refused' while
the operator saw an ordinary wafer. That is INV-M4-3's failure mode arriving through the
back door, and INV-M4-3 is the invariant that says a broken declaration must never be
indistinguishable from a working one.
So the pin covers the SURFACING, not the string. Two properties, both reachable from the
contract and both load-bearing at a named call site:
`basis_not_circle`  — `renderValidDieChip` hides the chip on exactly one condition,
`basis === 'circle'` (map_editor.js:5789 region). A refusal that
reported 'circle' would render a clean wafer with NO chip: the
silent fallback, wearing the right answer's face.
`reason_nonempty`   — the chip title, the toast and the console line are all built from
`validDie.reason`. An empty reason is a warning that says nothing,
which is how a user learns to ignore it. SCORED ONLY where the
reason comes from a function this harness actually runs; see
`$reason_source` on each case, and read the next paragraph.
WHAT THIS CONTRACT CANNOT SCORE, STATED RATHER THAN FAKED. `refused` is reached by three
routes and only one of them produces its reason inside a pure function. The other two
get theirs from `resolveValidDie` — async, network-bound, unreachable from any scorer.
An earlier draft of this group asserted `reason_nonempty` on all three; a mutation that
emptied the resolver's reason (`set('refused', null, '', ref)`) SURVIVED it, because the
string being checked was one the harness had written into its own fixture. That is the
copy-harness failure this repo has been bitten by before: a harness that re-types the
value it is scoring passes against an implementation that no longer produces it.
The assertion is therefore scoped to where it is real, and the resolver route is listed
as a RUNTIME-VERIFICATION item instead of being quietly counted as covered.
The chip's DOM — that it is inserted, and where — is CLIENT-ONLY surface with no server
counterpart, and it stays in `client2/tests/map_key_canonical_harness.mjs`. This contract
does not absorb it.
All three routes to `refused` are covered, because they arrive through different code:
an unresolvable reference, an unreadable declaration, and a reference that resolved to
zero cells.

valid_die_refused_render_divergence_case.name: unreadable_declaration
valid_die_refused_render_divergence_case.$why: Reaches `refused` through the PARSER, and it is the ONE route whose reason this contract can honestly score: `parseValidDieRef` is pure, the harness runs it, and the string asserted is the one the app would carry to the chip. A refusal built from a discarded parse error surfaces an empty explanation, and this vector is what fails.

valid_die_refused_render_divergence_case.name: unresolvable_ref
valid_die_refused_render_divergence_case.$why: The reason for this route is built inside `resolveValidDie` (async, network-bound), so NO scorer can reach it and this vector does not pretend to. Basis and passthrough ARE scored. The reason is a runtime-verification item — see the group comment; asserting it here would have meant asserting a string the harness itself wrote.

valid_die_refused_render_divergence_case.name: ref_resolved_to_zero_cells
valid_die_refused_render_divergence_case.$why: The third route, and the one that behaves differently: the client DERIVES `refused` from state (`basis: 'ref'` with an empty key set, map_editor.js:1919-1920) rather than being told, so no reason is attached at that point and the chip would render '⚠️ 유효 다이 맵 미해석' with an empty explanation. RECORDED, NOT ENDORSED. The app refuses upstream before this state can occur (map_editor.js:5751 region), so it is defence-in-depth today — but if that upstream guard is ever removed, this vector is what says the surfacing is thinner on this route than on the other two.

$comment: M4 INV-M4-4 — the ref key is a map identity, so it resolves through the SAME 7b
canonicalisation. A second normalisation here would reintroduce the exact bug 7b just
fixed, one layer down: the declaration says TPL_01, the meta row is TPL_1, and the
template silently fails to load.
Expected values are the 7b answers, referenced rather than restated — each case names the
`canonical_map_key_cases` entry it must agree with, and the scorers assert the agreement
rather than trusting the literal.

valid_die_ref_canonical_cases.name: string_declared_ref_key
valid_die_ref_canonical_cases.$why: Under a string declaration the ref key keeps its padding — the same input resolving two ways by declared type is what proves M4 is reusing 7b rather than reimplementing it.

$comment: M4② INV-M4-5 (SET AND UNSET) and the phase-2 half of INV-M4-1 (a map with no
declaration is unchanged). Written 2026-07-29, BEFORE either writer existed.
WHY A WRITER IS A CONTRACT SYMBOL AT ALL. Phase 1 could be scored entirely through the
READER, because phase 1 only read. Phase 2 writes, and a write is not scoreable through
the reader: hand-writing 'the meta after an unset' into a vector asserts nothing about
the code that produces it — it re-tests `parse(null)`, which `explicit_null` already
covers. So `apply_valid_die_ref` / `applyValidDieRef` are named in the symbol manifest
and the ROUND TRIP is scored THROUGH THE READER: apply, then ask the contract's own
`parse_valid_die_ref` and `resolve_valid_die_basis` what the result means. Nothing here
asserts the STORED SHAPE, on purpose — the contract does not get to pick between the
string form and the object form, only to insist that whichever is written reads back as
what was asked for.
WHY UNSET IS THE LOAD-BEARING DIRECTION. `valid_die_ref` lives inside
`wafer_map_metadata.grid_metadata`, a JSON payload with no user-facing editor. If the
authoring path can set it but not clear it, then nothing can clear it — the map is
pinned to a template forever, and if the template is also wrong the map is pinned to
`refused` forever. A feature that only scores the SET direction ships that state and
looks complete.
THE SPECIFIC WRONG IMPLEMENTATIONS THESE VECTORS DROP, each one a shape that passes a
set-only test:
a cleared text input written straight through as `valid_die_ref: ""`  -> reads `error`,
which by the phase-1 parse rule is a DECLARATION, so the map is refused permanently
and the UI offers no way back. `clear_writes_absence` and the two blank-key cases.
a clear implemented as 'skip the write'                              -> the old value
survives. `clear_after_set_returns_to_circle`.
a writer that rebuilds the meta from the fields it knows            -> every other key
is destroyed, and the falsy ones first. The base meta below declares `0`, `false`
and `""` deliberately: a `v || default` rebuild — the exact shape of known defect
D1, one layer up — turns `phys_edge_margin: 0` into 3.0 and moves the wafer mask of
a map that was only having its valid-die reference cleared.
a writer that mutates its argument                                   -> the editor's
cancel path silently keeps the edit. `input_not_mutated`, scored on every case.
a writer that emits `{map_id: k}` with no table                      -> that is the
ONE shape the two sides are RECORDED to read differently
(`valid_die_ref_home_divergence_cases.object_no_table_no_home`: server resolves,
client refuses). Authoring must not manufacture a split-brain declaration.
`no_tableless_object`, scored on every case.
BLANK KEY = CLEAR, and this is the one place the contract CHOSE between two defensible
answers (the other being 'reject the edit and leave the declaration alone'). Grounds:
INV-M4-5 is stated as 'unset returns source to circle', and in an editor the only way a
user submits a blank key IS by clearing the field. Both answers avoid the unrecoverable
state; only this one reaches `circle`, which is what the invariant names. Recorded here
rather than in a chat log so that overturning it is a contract edit.
PROOF THAT THESE VECTORS CAN GO RED (2026-07-29, both scorers, 8 named defects each,
each defect injected into the landed function rather than into a stand-in): a clear that
writes `""`, a clear that is a no-op, a `v || default` rebuild, a writer that mutates its
argument, one that emits a table-less object, one that refuses to clear an unreadable
declaration, one that only writes when the key is absent, and one that drops the declared
table. All eight fail on both sides. A vector nothing can break is not evidence.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: clear_writes_absence
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: INV-M4-1 through the SAVE path. A map that never declared a reference is saved by the same code that saves one that did — so the everyday case is 'the control is empty'. A writer that pipes an empty control through unconditionally puts `""` in the metadata of EVERY map anyone saves, and by the phase-1 parse rule every one of them is then `refused`. 이 벡터는 '선언 없는 맵은 오늘과 완전히 동일' 수용 기준이 저장 경로에서도 성립하는지를 본다.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: set_object_other_table
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: The cross-table form. Scored because the authoring UI's natural output is a picker over another table, and the table must survive the write — a writer that keeps only the key turns a cross-table reference into a same-table one pointing at a map that may not exist.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: clear_after_set_returns_to_circle
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: ⭐ INV-M4-5 itself, in two operations. This is the vector a set-only implementation fails: a clear written as 'don't touch it' leaves `TPL_1` in place and the readback is still `ref`. 지정만 채점하면 한 방향만 검증한 것이고, 운영에서는 되돌릴 수 없는 상태가 된다.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: round_trip_set_clear_set
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: ⭐ The full round trip the round was asked for. It drops two shapes a two-op test cannot see: a clear that leaves debris the next set appends to rather than replaces, and a set that refuses to write when it thinks a declaration already exists. `TPL_2` differs from `TPL_1` so 'the second set was a no-op' is visible.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: replace_existing_declaration
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: Re-pointing a map at a different template is re-declaration, not a first declaration. A writer that only fills an empty slot leaves `OLD_TPL` and the operator sees the new name in the UI while the old template is still the basis.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: clear_an_unreadable_declaration
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: ⭐ THE RECOVERY PATH. A map whose declaration is unreadable — a bad hand edit, a botched import — is `refused` on both sides and shows the operator nothing but a wafer with no mask. If the writer refuses to touch a declaration it cannot parse (a natural shape: parse first, then write), that map can never be repaired from the UI, and the metadata has no other editor. The clear path must not depend on the current value being readable.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: blank_key_is_a_clear
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: A whitespace-only key is what a user leaves behind by selecting the field contents and typing a space. The reader already calls this shape an ERROR when it reaches metadata (`whitespace_only_is_an_error`), so the writer is the only place it can be stopped. 헌장의 함정 목록: 빈 문자열과 0을 반드시 벡터에 넣는다.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: empty_key_is_a_clear
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: The declared empty string — the value a cleared `<input>` actually produces. Paired with `blank_key_is_a_clear` so that a writer trimming to `""` and one not trimming at all are both caught.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: empty_object_key_is_a_clear
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: The same blank arriving in the object form — a table picked, no map chosen. A writer that special-cases the string form and passes objects through verbatim writes `{table, map_id: ""}`, which the reader calls an error (`object_blank_map_id`), and the map is refused with a table name in it that makes the declaration look deliberate.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: unreadable_ref_argument_is_a_clear

$client_measured.how: the landed writer falls through its string and object branches to `return clear()`

valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: ⭐ A SEAM VECTOR FOR AN INPUT NO UI PRODUCES TODAY — which is the reason to pin it, not a reason to skip it. Two writers now answer this seam and NOTHING recorded what either says about a `ref` argument that is neither a key nor an object: the landed client CLEARS (measured, see `$client_measured`), and a server writer that validates before writing would plausibly RAISE. Today's UI cannot produce `5`; tomorrow's picker returning an id instead of a key can, and by then the disagreement is a production split-brain that nobody wrote down. GROUNDS FOR THE EXPECTED VALUE: an unreadable `ref` carries no key, and 'no key is a clear' is already contracted from INV-M4-5 by `blank_key_is_a_clear` / `empty_object_key_is_a_clear` — this is that rule applied to a third shape, not a mirror of whichever writer landed first. THIS VECTOR DOES NOT DECIDE THE QUESTION. 'Reject the edit' is the defensible alternative; if the server raises, both scorers print BOTH answers side by side and the Lead PM rules — which is the whole point of pinning it before the second writer lands rather than after.

valid_die_authoring_cases.name: preserves_every_other_key_including_declared_falsies
valid_die_authoring_cases.$why: ⭐ 선언된 0 함정. Every falsy value here is a LEGITIMATE DECLARATION: `phys_edge_margin: 0` (no edge exclusion — the axis known defect D1 already destroys on the client one layer down), `phys_offset_x: 0`, `grid_start_x: 0`, `grid_y_invert: false`, `auto_registered: false`, `some_future_key: ""`. A writer that rebuilds the meta from what it knows drops the keys it does not know; one that copies with `v || dflt` turns the zero margin into 3.0 and MOVES THE WAFER MASK of a map whose valid-die reference was merely being cleared. Both are silent. `binding` is here because it is a live additive key (§5.6-bis) that no phase-2 form has a control for — exactly the class phase 1's single passthrough line was a workaround for.

$comment: M4② INV-M4-6 — THE ONE-HOP LIMIT. Written 2026-07-29 before either guard existed.
A valid-die map is a map, so it can declare a `valid_die_ref` of its own. Two shapes
must be refused and today NEITHER IS: `resolve_valid_die_set` loads the referenced
map's meta and never asks what that map declares.
SELF-REFERENCE  A -> A. The map's own stored cells become its own validity criterion,
so every cell that exists is valid and every cell that does not is
invalid. That is not a mask, it is a tautology, and it looks like a
perfectly resolved reference in the chip.
TWO-LEVEL CHAIN A -> B where B -> C. B's STORED CELLS are used, but B has declared
that its own valid dies are C's — so the set A gets is one nobody
declared. The operator sees `ref` resolved and a plausible mask.
A cycle A -> B -> A needs no separate rule and no visited-set: B declares, therefore A
refuses. `two_cycle_refused` below is the vector that says so.
SCOREABILITY. The guard needs the REFERENCED map's metadata, which arrives from the DB
(server) or a fetch (client). Written inline at that call site it is unreachable by any
scorer, and a test that re-types the comparison scores zero — the trap this repo has
already hit with the DB-bound `src == TRANSFER_LOG_NONE`. So the contract
names an EXTRACTED pure predicate, `valid_die_chain_error(ref, ref_meta, home)`, and
both sides are held to the same answer on it.
'DECLARED' MEANS THE SAME THING HERE AS IN THE PARSER. Only `null`/absent is absence;
everything else is a declaration. That is not a new rule, it is the phase-1 rule
(`valid_die_ref_parse_cases`) applied one level down, and it is what the falsy vectors
below are for: `0` and `false` and `""` are declarations. Two wrong guards die here —
`if (refMeta.valid_die_ref)` (falsy test) and `parse(ref_meta)[0] is not None` (treats a
BROKEN declaration on the middle map as no declaration, which is the silent-fallback
shape INV-M4-3 forbids, one layer down).
IDENTITIES ARRIVE CANONICAL, AND THE GUARD ADDS NO NORMALISATION OF ITS OWN. Both the
reference key and the home key are already through `canonical_map_key` by the time the
resolver has them (server `_resolve_valid_die_uncached` does it before loading the
referenced meta; the client does it in `resolveValidDie`), so the predicate compares
canonical identities and nothing else. The mirrored pair
`self_reference_after_canonicalisation` / `padded_key_is_not_self_under_string` is what
holds that: the SAME declared text `LOT_01` against the SAME home key `LOT_1` canonicalises
to `LOT_1` under `slot: number` (self-reference) and stays `LOT_01` under `slot: string`
(a legitimate reference). A guard that strips its own zeros, lowercases, or otherwise
re-normalises fails the second — and a second normalisation is precisely what INV-M4-4
forbids. The scorers run the already-scored `canonical_map_key` rather than trusting the
vector's literal, and each case names the `canonical_map_key_cases` entry it agrees with.
WHAT THIS PAIR DOES NOT SCORE, stated rather than implied: that the CALLER canonicalises
before consulting the guard. That step is DB-bound on the server and network-bound on
the client, so no scorer reaches it; it is covered by `valid_die_ref_canonical_cases`
(INV-M4-4) at the resolver instead. Claiming it here would be the copy-harness failure —
the canonicalisation the scorer performs is the scorer's own.
VOCABULARY. `expect` is `ok` | `refused`, and a refusal carries `expect_kind`
(`self_reference` | `chain`) plus a NON-EMPTY reason — same discipline as INV-M4-3,
because a refusal nobody can read is a silent failure with extra steps. The WORDING is
deliberately NOT pinned: freezing a user-facing sentence into a contract makes every
copy edit a contract edit. `expect_kind` drives two things instead — the
fixture-inactivity guards (the group must keep carrying both refusal shapes) and the
assertion that the two kinds do not produce the SAME reason, since they are different
problems with different fixes (re-point the reference vs. flatten the template).
Field names differ across the seam by language convention (`map_id` server / `mapKey`
client); each scorer builds its own side's shape, exactly as the parse group does.
RECORDED AND NOT PINNED (Lead PM ruling, 2026-07-29). The landed client guard skips the
self-check when BOTH tables are `undefined` (`r.table !== undefined && h.table !==
undefined`). A server guard comparing them unconditionally would answer differently on
that input — but the input is unreachable: the declaring map's table is always known,
and the reference inherits it when the declaration omits it. Written down here so that
the next person to read the two guards side by side does not rediscover it as a finding,
and so that if the inheritance rule ever changes, the note is what says this became
reachable. No vector: a vector for an unreachable input costs a fixture on every future
edit and buys nothing. (Contrast `unreadable_ref_argument_is_a_clear` in the authoring
group, which IS pinned — that input is unreachable through today's UI but perfectly
reachable through tomorrow's, and the two writers can already answer it differently.)
PROOF THAT THESE VECTORS CAN GO RED (2026-07-29, both scorers, 10 named defects each):
a falsy `if (ref_meta.valid_die_ref)` guard, a `parse(...) is not None` guard, a
key-PRESENCE guard, a self-check that re-normalises, one that compares keys only, one
that compares tables only, a guard refusing unknown referenced metadata, one reason for
both kinds, a reasonless refusal, and a guard refusing everything. All ten fail on both
sides. The run also found a hole in the CLIENT HARNESS rather than in the client: the
chain guard's helper `validDieRefDisplay` was missing from `client_symbols`, so the
extracted function threw, the harness recorded the exception text as the refusal reason,
and 'one reason for both kinds' passed. The helper is now in the manifest and a THROWN
extraction is a hard failure (`threw()` in the harness). A vector nothing can break is
not evidence, and neither is a harness that scores its own stack traces.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: plain_one_hop_ok
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: The negative control, and it is not decorative: without it a guard that refuses every reference passes this whole group and disables the feature the round is shipping.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: ref_meta_unknown_is_not_a_chain_error
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: An unregistered referenced map IS refused — by `align_unavailable`, upstream of this predicate and already contracted (`_resolve_valid_die_uncached`: '참조 맵의 규격이 미등록'). Refusing again here with a chain reason would give one state two vocabularies on one seam, which is the mistake `circle|map|unresolved` vs `circle|ref|refused` already cost this contract once. The predicate answers only the question it owns.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: ref_declares_null_is_not_a_chain
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: `null` is absence at every level (the phase-1 rule). A guard using `'valid_die_ref' in ref_meta` — key presence rather than value — refuses this legitimate reference, and the operator is told their template is a chain when it is not.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: two_level_chain_refused
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: ⭐ The chain itself. Today this resolves silently to TPL_1's stored cells — a set the operator did not declare, wearing a resolved reference's chip.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: two_cycle_refused
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: A -> B -> A. Listed to show the 1-hop rule SUBSUMES cycle detection: no visited set, no recursion depth, no traversal. If a future implementation reaches for a cycle detector, this vector is already green and the detector is a second answer to a question already answered.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: chain_with_a_broken_declaration_refused
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: ⭐ The middle map has a declaration and it is broken. A guard written as `parse(ref_meta)[0] is not None` sees `(None, error)` and concludes 'no declaration', so it uses the cells of a map whose OWN validity is refused. That is the phase-1 silent fallback exactly, one level down: an unreadable declaration folded into absence.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: chain_declared_zero_refused
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: ⭐ 선언된 0. `if (refMeta.valid_die_ref)` is the shortest way to write this guard and it is wrong for exactly three values — `0`, `false`, `""` — all of which are declarations under the phase-1 rule and all of which are present in this group. Same falsy-substitution shape as known defect D1, in a new place.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: chain_declared_false_refused
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: `false` reads like 'no, do not use a reference' and is a declaration all the same — the mirror of `boolean_is_an_error` in the parse group, which refuses `true` for the same reason.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: self_reference_refused
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: ⭐ A -> A. The map's own cells become its own validity criterion, which is true by construction and therefore says nothing — and it resolves, so the chip reports a healthy reference over a mask that is just 'the cells that exist'. Easy to author by accident: the picker lists the map you are editing.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: self_reference_after_canonicalisation
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: ⭐ INV-M4-7 reuse, first polarity. Under `slot: number` the declared `LOT_01` canonicalises to the home key `LOT_1`, so this is self-reference wearing a different spelling — the same class of miss 7b was created to fix (`client 'LOT_01' vs server 'LOT_1'`). The scorer runs `canonical_map_key` rather than trusting the literal, so if 7b's answer ever changed this vector would move with it instead of quietly disagreeing.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: padded_key_is_not_self_under_string
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: ⭐ The other polarity, and the load-bearing one. SAME declared text, SAME home key, opposite answer, and the only thing that changed is the declared column type: under `slot: string` the canonical reference key is `LOT_01`, which is NOT the home identity `LOT_1`. This is the vector a guard with its own normalisation fails — strip the zeros, lowercase, or 'helpfully' compare loosely and it reports a self-reference where there is a perfectly ordinary one. A second normalisation is exactly what INV-M4-4 forbids, and this is where it surfaces.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: same_key_other_table_is_not_self
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: Map identity is `(table, map_key)`, never the key alone (SPEC §6 '계획 정체성'). A guard comparing keys only refuses a perfectly ordinary cross-table reference — and cross-table is the commonest authoring shape, a product template table referenced from a lot map.

valid_die_chain_cases.name: same_table_other_key_is_not_self
valid_die_chain_cases.$why: The other half of 'identity is the pair': a guard comparing tables only refuses every same-table reference, which is the inheritance case the declaration syntax was built around (`string_inherits_home_table`).

$comment: 🔴 THE LAST DECISION BEFORE THE DATABASE. Added 2026-07-29 after a QA NO-GO on M4②,
and the reason it did not exist is the most useful thing in this file.
WHAT WAS SCORED AND WHAT WAS NOT. `valid_die_authoring_cases` scores the PURE WRITER
`applyValidDieRef` — 402 green assertions, 19 mutations caught, and it is a correct
function. But a pure writer only decides WHAT to write once something has decided that
a write should happen AT ALL, and that second decision lives in `validDieRefForPush`,
which was in no contract. A green pure writer was read — by me — as 'the write path is
scored'. It was not, and a HIGH defect lived in the gap:
syncValidDieRefControls: a declared table not present in the <select> options is
forced to `''` (correct on its own — it refuses to show an option that is not
there, and its comment promises `raw` is preserved).
validDieRefForPush:      reads that `''` as 'the user chose the home table'
(correct on its own — `''` is genuinely the inherit-the-home-table choice).
together:                an UNTOUCHED Push silently demotes a cross-table
declaration. `{"table":"tpl_map","map_id":"TPL_1"}` is SAVED as `"TPL_1"`.
The table is gone, the chip still reports a healthy reference, and nothing on
screen says a stored value changed.
Two functions, each right in isolation, and nobody scored the round trip. That is the
same defect shape as the two HIGH findings that caused this file to exist — arriving
this time BETWEEN two functions on ONE side of the seam rather than across it. A seam
is not only server-vs-client.
THE VECTORS MAY NOT SET CONTROL VALUES DIRECTLY, and this is the load-bearing rule of
the group. The round harness did `el.validDieRefTable.value = table`, skipping
`syncValidDieRefControls` — so it asserted a control state THE APP CANNOT PRODUCE and
was green while the contract between the two functions was entirely unscored. A scorer
that writes the value it is about to read is testing its own fixture. Every case here
supplies only what the APP supplies — `validDie.raw` and the option LIST — then calls
`syncValidDieRefControls`, and applies a user edit only where a user really would.
EXPECTATIONS ARE READBACKS, not shapes. What is asserted is what the SAVED payload
means when read by `parseValidDieRef` — the same vocabulary as the authoring group. The
decision object (`keep`) is asserted alongside it so that a change in what `keep` means
cannot pass by moving the logic into the glue.
CLIENT-ONLY, and NOT because the server is exempt. The server has no counterpart to a
DOM control reflecting a stored value, so there is nothing to score against. The
server's half of the same invariant is `valid_die_authoring_cases`, which both sides run.
THE COMPOSITION IS RUN, NOT RE-TYPED — resolved 2026-07-29, within the round. This
group first scored the Push composition by REPRODUCING the two glue lines from the Push
site, because they lived inside a DOM-bound function no scorer could reach. That was
declared as a known duplication and the fix was requested as the `pending` symbol
`valid_die_ref_payload`. map-pm extracted it, the copy in the scorer was deleted in the
same pass, and the group now calls the same function the app calls. An extraction that
lands while the scorer keeps its copy buys nothing: the copy is the thing that goes
stale. `expect_keep` remains asserted alongside the readback so the composition cannot
absorb a change in what `keep` means.
⭐ ONE ASSERTION HERE IS `===`, NOT VALUE EQUALITY: `payload_is_the_untouched_grid_meta_
object`. INV-M4-1 says an undeclared, untouched map's payload is byte-identical to
`2a9f6c4`, and that is a claim about the OBJECT. Measured: an implementation returning
`{ ...gridMeta }` instead of `gridMeta` satisfies EVERY other assertion in this group —
the readback, the key check, the preserved-keys check — and is caught by this one and
nothing else. A copy silently downgrades 'we did not touch it' to 'we rebuilt the same
keys in the same order', which stays true only until someone adds a key, reorders one,
or lets a `v || dflt` through.
2026-08-04 - THE TABLE PICKER IS GONE, AND WHAT THAT DID TO THIS GROUP
User ruling: a valid-die map is ALWAYS stored in `valid_die_ref`, so the <select> that
chose its table was removed. Two cases here described choices the UI can no longer
express (`user_repoints_to_another_table`, `user_inherits_the_home_table`) and they are
retired with the control. `table_options` is retired with them.
🔴 THE INVARIANT DID NOT RETIRE - IT MOVED. The QA finding this group exists for was:
two functions, each right on its own, together rewriting a declaration the user never
touched. The <select> was the mechanism, not the invariant. The same defect is now one
line away in the other direction: implement 'the table is fixed' as 'always write
valid_die_ref' and an UNTOUCHED save repoints every declaration authored before the
ruling. That is not hypothetical - the live wafer_map_metadata holds 8 such rows (7 bare
strings and 1 explicit object, resolving to `bonding_map` x7 and `dt_map` x1), and both
`bonding_map` and `valid_die_ref` carry maps, so a repointed declaration can land on a
real map nobody declared. The screen stays healthy.
So the axis this group holds open is now: an untouched declaration naming a table OTHER
than the fixed one must come out of a save byte-identical, while a key the user actually
changed must come out naming the fixed table. Both halves are required - an
implementation that only preserves would never move anything to `valid_die_ref`, and an
implementation that only moves is the defect above.
STILL CLIENT-ONLY, and for the same reason: the server has no counterpart to a DOM
control reflecting a stored value. `parseValidDieRef` - the STORAGE FORMAT's meaning,
which both sides run - was deliberately NOT changed by this ruling. A bare string still
means 'a map in MY table' on both sides (`valid_die_ref_parse_cases`), because changing
that reading is what would silently repoint the same 8 rows on the SERVER too.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: legacy_cross_table_declaration_untouched_save
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: ⭐ THE AXIS, re-anchored 2026-08-04. `tpl_map` is a table other than the fixed `valid_die_ref` - the shape of all 8 declarations that exist in the live database today. A save in which the user touched NOTHING must write back what was stored. GROUNDS: INV-M4-1. 손대지 않은 저장이 저장 값을 바꾸면, 사용자가 하지 않은 편집이 사용자 이름으로 기록된다.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: fixed_table_declaration_untouched_save
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: The control, and it is not decorative: it is the ONLY difference from the case above - whether the stored declaration already names the fixed table. If both pass, preservation has been shown NOT to depend on which table was named. If only this one passes, the implementation is rewriting the rows that disagree, which is the defect. A no-op save is a no-op on every row, agreeing or not.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: empty_string_declaration_is_clearable
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: ⭐ THE DEAD END. A stored `""` is a DECLARATION under the phase-1 parse rule, so the map is `refused` on both sides — and `map_overlay`'s own docstring names that the state with no way back (`되돌릴 길이 없는 상태`). This UI was supposed to be the way back. But the controls show an EMPTY key box (correct — there is no key to show), so the screen matches the stored value, `keep` fires, and the `""` is written straight back. Typing a key and clearing it again lands in the same place. There is no sequence of user actions that clears it. What is asserted is only the OUTCOME — the saved payload must read as `none` — because how to get there (never write back an unreadable raw / treat a blank control as a clear) is the implementer's call, not the contract's.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: null_declaration_stays_absent
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: The paired shape QA asked for, and the one that is already correct — which is why it belongs here. `null` reads as absence, so preserving it is harmless and the map is on circle either way. Kept as the negative control for the case above: it proves the assertion is 'the saved value must read as none', not 'never keep', so a fix that stops keeping ANYTHING would be caught by the two untouched-push cases above.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: absent_declaration_untouched_push
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: INV-M4-1 at its strictest: a map that never declared anything must produce a payload with NO `valid_die_ref` key at all — not `null`, not `""`. ⭐ `expect_payload_is_the_same_object` is scored with `===`, NOT by value, and that is the point: 'byte-identical to 2a9f6c4' is a claim about the OBJECT, and a value comparison passes against an implementation returning `{ ...gridMeta }`. A copy that happens to agree today has quietly changed the claim from 'we did not touch it' to 'we rebuilt the same keys in the same order' — which is only true until someone adds a key, reorders one, or lets a `v || dflt` through. The two assertions are different strengths of the same invariant and both are kept: `expect_payload_has_key` says nothing was ADDED, identity says nothing was REBUILT.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: unreadable_declaration_untouched_push_is_preserved
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: The one case where preserving an UNREADABLE declaration is right, and it is why `keep` exists at all. The user did not touch the field; silently rewriting their broken declaration into a tidy string would destroy the only evidence of what they mistyped. Note the deliberate contrast with `clear_an_unreadable_declaration` in the authoring group: there the USER clears it and it must clear; here nobody touched it and it must survive. The two together say the writer follows the user rather than tidying up behind them.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: user_clears_the_key
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: INV-M4-5 through the REAL path rather than through the pure writer: state, sync, edit, decide, write, read back. The authoring group proves `applyValidDieRef(meta, null)` clears; this proves that emptying the key box actually reaches that call.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: user_declares_on_a_previously_absent_map
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: First declaration on a map that had none - the path the whole M4-2 round exists to open, and since 2026-08-04 the assertion that a NEW designation carries the FIXED table rather than inheriting the canvas table. `home_table` is deliberately NOT `valid_die_ref` here: an implementation that emitted the bare-string (inherit) form would read back as `seam_map` and fail.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: user_rekeys_a_legacy_declaration_onto_the_fixed_table
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: ⭐ THE OTHER HALF OF THE AXIS. Without it, 'never rewrite an untouched declaration' is satisfiable by never writing anything, and the ruling would be unimplemented while this group stayed green. A key the user actually changed is a NEW designation, and a new designation is a `valid_die_ref` one - the old table does not survive the choice that replaced it. Paired with `legacy_cross_table_declaration_untouched_save`, which has the same stored value and differs ONLY in whether the user typed.

valid_die_push_decision_cases.name: retyping_the_same_key_is_not_an_edit
valid_die_push_decision_cases.$why: The boundary between the two cases above, and the one a careless implementation gets wrong. 'The user typed' is not an edit - 'the value differs from what was stored' is. Typing back the key that was already showing must not move the declaration, or every user who clicks into the field to READ it repoints their own map by leaving.
